summary: Deep technical review of quantization tradeoffs (INT8, FP8, GPTQ, AWQ) focusing on runtime implications with KV cache and batching under VPC/on-prem constraints. We validated a hypothesis that KV-cache warmup + batching interacts with precision fallback and observed a repeatable accuracy delta on a small subset of prompts. Actionable plan: per-layer bisect tests, reproduce on Vesper on-prem spec, and run canary with sticky KV disabled.
topics: INT8 vs FP8 vs GPTQ vs AWQ accuracy tradeoffs
Runtime throughput and latency impact of quantized kernels
KV cache warmup, staleness, and sticky KV behavior
VPC/on-prem binary/kernel compatibility and kernel selection
Fallbacks, canary rollout, and bisect plan for regressions
transcript:
Header: 2025-09-02 16:00 PDT | Duration: ~62m
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Vesper ML Infra Lead), Samir Patel (Vesper CTO), Lina Gomez (Vesper ML Eng)
Artifacts referenced: quant-playbook.pdf (internal), perf-dashboard CSV (/sheets/perf-vesper-q3.csv), canary-config.yaml (link shared in chat).

[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we're gonna dive into the stress test results you sent over. Quick roll call?
[00:12] Jordan: Jordan here. We have Samir and Lina as well. Thanks Alex.
[00:18] Alex: Cool. Priya from infra and performance is with me. Priya, you wanna kick off with what we saw in the runtime traces?
[00:24] Priya: Sure. So we ran the baseline across four precision paths: FP16 baseline, INT8 quantized, GPTQ post-train, and AWQ variant. We measured p50/p95 token latency, throughput at 8/16/32 batch widths, and KV cache hit patterns. The main failure mode we saw was small-accuracy deltas in GPTQ and AWQ on a subset of long-context prompts when KV cache was sticky and batching high.
[00:48] Lina: Sorry can I interrupt, when you say "sticky" KV do you mean cached prefixes are persisted across requests for the same session?
[00:55] Priya: Yeah sticky KV meaning the KV cache is reused aggressively across incoming tokens for the session, which reduces compute but can produce divergent hidden state when quantized kernels reorder arithmetic a bit.
[01:12] Jordan: We reproduced that locally too, but only on like 2-3% of prompts. Most traffic looks fine. It's the rare long instruction-following examples where output diverges.
[01:26] Alex: Good, that matches what we saw. Let's talk through possible root causes — rounding noise, kernel math order, and KV staleness interactions. Priya, did the perf traces show any correlation with sequence length or batch queuing time?
[01:41] Priya: There is a clear correlation with effective sequence length > 1024 and batch coalescing latency. When the runtime coalesces many requests into a single kernel launch, the INT8/GPTQ kernels use fused kernels that sometimes change the accumulation order. That plus KV reuse seems to push some activations over quantization boundaries.
[02:05] Samir: So this isn't purely a model accuracy regression at training time, it's emergent from the runtime and precision mix?
[02:11] Priya: Exactly. The model weights are the same; it's numerical sensitivity at inference time across quantized math paths.
[02:18] Alex: We discussed four mitigations in the notes: per-layer dequant on suspect layers, slightly higher calibration for problematic layers, disable sticky KV for canary, or use FP8 fallback for the last N layers. Which of these is least invasive for Vesper's latency SLO?
[02:36] Lina: Disabling sticky KV will increase token compute and hurt p50 but might be acceptable for the canary if it's only enabled for a small percentage of traffic.
[02:44] Jordan: We can't lose p95 for real-time ops though. Our SLA is 150ms p95. We need the canary to not blow up latency.
[02:52] Priya: If we do a canary at 5% with sticky KV off, p95 increased by ~28% in the tests but still under the SLA on the dedicated GPU they provided. However in on-prem smaller boxes it would be tight.
[03:11] Alex: Right, so we need to validate on your on-prem spec. Samir, did you confirm the node GPU and driver details?
[03:18] Samir: We have a 32GB A6000 equivalent with driver 525 and CUDA 12.1, but the node is behind our VPC with strict container policies (no custom kernel modules). We can't load vendor-supplied jit libs that change the math path easily.
[03:34] Priya: That's important because some AWQ/GPTQ kernels rely on custom compiled kernels or ff kernels. On the hosted side we can choose optimized kernels; on-prem we might fall back to generic kernels that are slower. That could change which precision path is viable.
[03:50] Jordan: Is there a way to force a deterministic kernel ordering to avoid math reorder?
[03:55] Priya: We're exploring a "deterministic accumulation" flag that makes kernels use a fixed reduction order at the cost of ~8-12% throughput. For canary it may be fine.
[04:07] Lina: How about FP8? We saw FP8 had smaller divergence but was slower than INT8 in some cases?
[04:13] Priya: FP8 (E4M3-ish) has better dynamic range and typically fewer edge-case flips than INT8, but the runtime on your node doesn't have the newest fused FP8 kernels—so in our tests FP8 latency was 1.2-1.5x FP16 baseline on your spec. GPTQ tended to be fastest but most numerically sensitive.
[04:34] Alex: Quick sanity check: AWQ vs GPTQ, were the deltas concentrated on specific attention layers or feedforward layers?
[04:41] Priya: Our per-layer diff heatmap (we'll share the CSV) shows a pattern: layers 18-22 (mid-high attention blocks) had the highest sensitivity. That hints at attention softmax / scaling sensitivity to small bit flips.
[04:56] Jordan: OK, so per-layer dequant or mixing precisions in those layers might solve accuracy without global FP8.
[05:03] Samir: If we mix precision, can the runtime select layerwise kernels automatically?
[05:07] Priya: Yes, Redwood runtime supports layerwise profiles. We can specify a precision map in the model config so layers 0-17 run INT8 and 18-22 run FP8 or FP16, then rest INT8. The challenge is we need to validate cache coherency in that mixed path.
[05:24] Alex: Let's talk about KV cache specifics. In the failing traces, was the KV cache being updated with quantized states or dequantized states?
[05:33] Priya: The runtime stores KV in quantized form to save memory by default. For canary we tried dequantizing KV when writing back to cache for the problematic sessions which reduced divergence but increased memory and write CPU.
[05:46] Lina: Dequantizing KV on write sounds heavy. How much memory uplift?
[05:49] Priya: In our test it increased memory by ~30% for long sessions. On your cluster that means you'd need an extra 6-8GB per GPU for peak loads.
[05:59] Jordan: Not ideal. We don't have spare headroom.
[06:02] Alex: Another angle—KV aging and staleness. Could cached keys be slightly stale vs recomputed keys due to different batching orders?
[06:10] Priya: Yes, if requests are fused in different micro-batches across runs, the sequence of accumulation can differ and the cached K/V pairs represent a particular numeric path. With quantization, those small differences amplify.
[06:24] Samir: Does disabling batch coalescing for sessions with sticky KV help?
[06:28] Priya: It reduces throughput but improves determinism. We measured p95 increases but error rates dropped for the sensitive prompts.
[06:36] Jordan: So for canary we could route 5% of traffic to a path that disables batch coalescing and sticky KV, or disable sticky KV only. Which is simpler?
[06:44] Priya: Disabling sticky KV is simpler to implement quickly in your VPC, since it only toggles cache policy. Disabling coalescing is more invasive to the runtime scheduler.
[06:53] Alex: On the topic of VPC/on-prem kernel availability, can you confirm whether your security policy allows installing Redwood's fused kernel package?
[07:01] Samir: Our policy doesn't allow arbitrary kernel modules, but we can run user-space jit libs if signed and scanned. We need a list of library checksums.
[07:11] Alex: We'll provide vetted artifacts and checksums. Also, we can provide a container image that uses only standard runtime paths if that's preferable.
[07:20] Lina: Let's also talk about the regression triage flow you recommended.
[07:24] Priya: We propose a four-step triage: 1) Bisect (per-layer GPTQ/AWQ toggles) to narrow suspect layers, 2) Reproduce on identical on-prem spec disabling sticky KV to rule out cache interaction, 3) Run mixed-precision profile to confirm repair, 4) Canary rollout with sticky KV disabled for 5% traffic + monitoring.
[07:44] Jordan: For bisect, how long will that take? We have hundreds of layers on our 30B model.
[07:50] Priya: With automated scripts it takes ~6-10 hours per run on one node; parallelizing across 4 nodes gets it down to about 2.5 hours. We'll help with orchestration.
[07:59] Samir: We can provision a temporary 4-node test cluster.
[08:03] Alex: Good. Priya, earlier you mentioned a deterministic accumulation flag. If we enable that, what's the perf hit and does it remove the need for layerwise FP8?
[08:12] Priya: Perf hit is roughly 8-12% for many workloads. In tests with deterministic accumulation, the divergence almost disappeared on GPTQ for most prompts. It may be enough for the canary while we do a proper per-layer fix.
[08:28] Lina: If deterministic mode works, can we enable it selectively only for the sensitive layers?
[08:33] Priya: Not currently; it's a global kernel flag. But we can implement an intermediate step: dequantize cache for sessions that hit sensitive layers. Slightly messy but doable.
[08:44] Jordan: Regarding monitoring, what metrics should we track in canary?
[08:48] Alex: We'll push specific signal sets: token-level perplexity delta, exact-match on golden prompts, p50/p95 latency, KV hit rate, and a divergence score that flags when generated sequence probability mass shifts beyond threshold. We'll hook those to your perf dashboard.
[09:05] Samir: Excellent. For SSO and audit reasons we need to log model version and kernel checksum with each trace. Can we surface that?
[09:12] Priya: Yes, runtime includes kernel tags in trace metadata. We'll ensure it's in logs.
[09:18] Lina: A few practical questions: 1) How do we run GPTQ on our on-prem box? 2) What are AWQ licensing or runtime dependencies?
[09:27] Priya: GPTQ is a post-training quantization artifact we provide scripts for; it's run offline and produces quantized weights. AWQ variant is similar but uses a different quantization scheme; both are open-source but the runtime needs the fused kernels for optimal perf. On your box we can use a conservative quantized artifact that avoids custom kernels but is a bit larger.
[09:45] Jordan: If custom kernels are a blocker can we fallback to INT8 but with per-layer calibration adjustments?
[09:51] Priya: Yes, we can attempt per-layer re-calibration — slightly shifting zero-points and scales for suspect layers. It sometimes fixes edge cases without changing kernels.
[10:00] Alex: Let's capture clear next steps and owners.
[10:04] Jordan: Quick note — we also want to test with a synthetic trace that increases context to 2048 to surface edge cases.
[10:10] Priya: We'll add that to the bisect run.

Recap and decisions:
- Immediate canary: 5% traffic, sticky KV disabled for canary sessions, deterministic accumulation OFF initially. Monitor divergence signals and latency (Alex will share dashboard).
- Parallel bisect: Priya + Redwood infra will run per-layer GPTQ/AWQ delta tests on a 4-node test cluster; goal to identify layers 18-22 sensitivity and propose precision mix.
- On-prem validation: Jordan/Samir to provide exact node spec and confirm what kernel/jit libs are allowed. Redwood to supply signed artifacts and checksums.
- Fallback options: dequantize KV on write (memory cost), layerwise FP8/FP16 for specific layers, or deterministic accumulation global flag (throughput hit).

[10:35] Alex: Anything else?
[10:38] Samir: Small ask — can you include a one-page playbook listing quick toggles to try in order?
[10:44] Priya: Yes, we'll send a triage playbook with commands and expected impact.
[10:48] Jordan: Thanks everyone. This was helpful.
[10:51] Alex: Great, we'll follow up with the CSV and orchestration play for bisect. Meeting adjourned.

Notes on transcript: occasional ASR errors ("K V cash" for KV cache, "Redwood Dedicate" for Redwood Dedicated) and some speaker label drift where system labeled a short interjection as "Speaker 3" — corrected where obvious.
